item.title: Naked at Last: A Conversation with F. Keith Wahle
item.dc:creator: Joseph Grantham
item.description: “When I carried this in from the funeral home, I thought, This is the kind of bag that a magician would make live doves fly out of.”
item.content:encoded:
Photograph courtesy of F. Keith Wahle.

When the poet F. Keith Wahle was first published in The Paris Review, he was working at the Cincinnati Public Library. He’d lived in Cincinnati for almost his whole life. A conscientious objector during Vietnam, he completed his service as an orderly for two years in a psych ward at the same hospital where he was born. The only time Wahle didn’t live in the Cincinnati area was when he attended the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, where he studied with the poets Donald Justice, Mark Strand, and Larry Levis. And then he was back in Cincinnati, where a librarian named Beth, who later became his wife of fifty-two years, helped get him a job. They worked in the same building for three decades.

The first poem he contributed to the Review was “Sonnet”—a poem that is not a sonnet but takes up the sonnet form as its subject. The Review published three more of his poems in the mid-to-late seventies, during Michael Benedikt’s tenure as poetry editor. Much of Wahle’s work is unsettling. When I mailed a copy of his 1998 collection A Choice of Killers to a filmmaker friend in Baltimore, she told me she couldn’t read it at night, which is not something you often hear about a poetry collection, outside of, maybe, Poe’s. At the same time, the poems are colorful, hallucinatory, and incredibly funny. They’re full of gags (Wahle is a fan of Laurel and Hardy and of W. C. Fields); they’re sometimes cartoonish (he’s an avid collector of Walt Kelly’s Pogo comic strip); and they’re often, as he puts it, “erotically obsessed.”

Photograph courtesy of F. Keith Wahle.

In the years since his poems appeared in the Review, Wahle has published chapbooks and full-length collections with small and micro presses, but, to this day, his work has never gained a wide audience. I visited Wahle in Ohio this year, just four months after his wife died. We sat in his living room, surrounded by stacks of DVDs (many still in their original packaging) and Christmas decorations (it was June). A couple of hours into our conversation, I realized that Beth’s urn was sitting in a velvet drawstring bag at our feet. Wahle held up the bag. “When I carried this in from the funeral home, I thought, This is the kind of bag that a magician would make live doves fly out of.”

Later that evening, Wahle showed me a couple of home movies on his television. One was sixteen-millimeter footage he’d taken in the seventies of various lovers trying on brightly colored underwear or emerging from bubble baths covered in suds. Another was from 2011—a recording of a Beckettian piece Wahle had written and performed in his hometown, titled Can Anyone Hear? The show begins with a blindfolded Wahle crawling onstage in front of a live audience and describing a series of haunting scenes: a woman on the street who pees her pants for money, two men in overcoats walking into a lake until they’re consumed by the water, a woman with a pair of scissors protruding from her forehead. Every few minutes, Wahle pauses and calls out, “Can anyone hear me? Can anyone hear what I’m saying?” By the end of the performance, he is completely nude except for his blindfold.

Photograph courtesy of F. Keith Wahle.

 

INTERVIEWER

You’ve mentioned that you don’t use a computer at home. Do you own a computer?

F. KEITH WAHLE

I have a laptop and I have a printer. My plan was to use the laptop to compile manuscripts. When I bought it, I consulted with a woman who used to work at the library. This was about a decade ago. She really knew her stuff. She said, “I think you’d be happier with an Apple.” So I got an Apple computer. But I’d already compiled the manuscript for No More Poems at the library. And they have the Word program there. Well, when I opened up the laptop I’d bought, it had a different version of Word, which wasn’t compatible with the program I’d been using. I would have had to correct a lot of poems.

INTERVIEWER

How long did you mess with the laptop before you decided not to use it?

WAHLE

About a minute. See, I came up using a typewriter. And a typewriter has a lot of limitations, but it’s very intuitive. Even an electronic typewriter, which has some quirks, is still mostly intuitive. My issue with composing, or even formatting things, on a computer is that there are too many options. It renders everything counterintuitive. I’ve also found that, at the library, when I’m using the computer and something happens that I don’t understand, all I have to do is turn over my shoulder and there’s somebody who can help me. If the same thing happened at home, I’d just be stuck. I know a lot of people would think I’m a complete primitive. But that’s the way I like it.

INTERVIEWER

Do you ever find that your poems and your real life bleed into each other?

WAHLE

I don’t write from experience, except on a few rare occasions. But, on the other hand, I’m always writing from experience. When I start writing, the experiences come in little bits and pieces. I could have a one-page poem and buried in there is something that actually happened and another thing that might’ve happened and another thing that happened in a movie I saw. Experience is not always just what you’ve done. It’s also the movies you’ve watched and the plays you’ve seen and the music you’ve listened to. In my poems, there’s a sort of uneasy mix of the personal and the impersonal and the improbable. Every poem I write is completely personal, but that doesn’t mean it really happened.

INTERVIEWER

I imagine working in the psych ward must’ve had some impact on your writing.

WAHLE

Some of the extreme things I saw did feed into what I was doing with poetry. We had a lot of alcoholics on the ward, and they’d get the shakes in the morning. But only a few of them really flipped over into the heavy-duty hallucinations, and that was very weird. If you ever saw a person having delirium tremens, you would never think of having an alcoholic drink again.

There was one guy I was trying to feed, and I couldn’t get him to eat anything on his tray. But he had some ice cream in a little insulated dish, and I thought, “I can maybe get a few spoonfuls of this down.” So I gave him a few spoonfuls of the ice cream. But he kept touching his tongue and saying, “There’s dog hairs in this.” At one point he looked over, in the corner of the room by the door, and he said, “Is that a grizzly bear over there or is that just Smokey the Bear?” 

INTERVIEWER

Were you able to write on the clock when you worked at the library?

WAHLE

I wrote all the time. I stole time from the library like crazy. I had a typewriter at my desk. I had legitimate letters I needed to type for library business, but I also wrote a lot of personal correspondence and rough drafts of poems. I tried to fly under the radar. I wasn’t that nefarious about it. I think I was a pretty good worker, actually. But if I had a slump time, I didn’t go looking for stuff I could’ve been doing. Sometimes I would just jot something down. I wrote most of the poems in those “unpoem” collections during my lunch hour. I would usually go up and get something out of the vending machine. Some of the tables were library carrels, so you could have some privacy.

INTERVIEWER

Why do you call them “unpoems”?

WAHLE

A lot of my poems are pretty long, at least two or three pages. Like “Sonnet,” and “Secrets.” At the time, I was finding myself more and more driven to write longer and longer poems. They would get to be pages long. And I’d realize they were total crap. Nothing went together. They weren’t going to be salvageable, as far as I could tell. So I thought, One remedy might be to deliberately write short poems. 

Because I was writing them during my lunch hour, I was writing by hand. Previously I’d almost always composed on the typewriter. I started thinking, Let’s see if I can write a poem in just one sitting. And, Let me try to write a poem in one sitting and then not revise it, not even think about revising it. I rarely do more than three or four revisions, anyway. But the idea was to push that even farther—not doing any revisions if possible. Or if I did, one word or one line.

I did revise some. I broke all my own rules. Sometimes I’d work on a poem for two or three days, or I’d write a poem quickly and then still do some revisions. But I called them unpoems because I thought they were the opposite of what people would consider a well-made poem.

INTERVIEWER

Is doing no more than three or four revisions a general rule for you?

WAHLE

In general, if I did more than six revisions, something was really wrong. At the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, people would say things like, “Oh yeah, I revised this about thirty times.” There was one guy—I don’t remember his name and that’s probably for the best. But every time he turned in a poem for a workshop, before he read it, he would say, “Oh, I made a couple of revisions on this.” We were supposed to get out our pens and cross things out and add things in. But the revisions were always something like, he’d changed a line break by three words or he’d changed one word in the whole poem. On some level, I felt like he was kidding us, that this was like a technique of his to get us to take his work more seriously. Maybe more seriously than he took it. 

But I had this image of the well-made poem, and that was never what I thought I was doing. With the unpoems, I was deliberately moving myself away not only from the way I had worked for years but the way I thought other people worked.

INTERVIEWER

You decided to lean into what was making you feel self-conscious.

WAHLE

I was feeling more and more separated, like, Everybody who writes poems does this more carefully than I do. Which I think is not true. But I had this feeling that everybody else was trying to polish their poems to jewellike clarity and I was just typing!

Truman Capote’s famous statement about Norman Mailer was something like, He isn’t really a writer, he’s just a typist. In my mind, I was more of a typist than the other poets, who I imagined were taking twenty minutes to polish a single line. I was pushing myself to write faster, to be more spontaneous. I wanted, a little bit, to be saying, I’m not really a writer, I’m just a typist. Saying, in other words, that these were just spontaneous imaginings and improvisations.

INTERVIEWER

Tell me about the origin of “Sonnet.” The poem begins, “You realize, even as you start this / that it won’t end up as a sonnet.” 

WAHLE

I had all sorts of prejudices about putting titles on poems. For example, a lot of modern poets like to make the title of the poem the first line. I always thought that was a horrible idea. I always thought the title should be a title and the first line should be a first line. I also rebelled against titles that were simply a description of what kind of poem it was. So, a sonnet called “Sonnet,” I thought, was kind of ridiculous. Or a villanelle called “Villanelle.” Or a poem that’s just called “Poem.” And perhaps the silliest of all, a haiku called “Haiku.” Then, I went to a poetry reading that John Ashbery did and he read a sonnet that was thirteen lines long. And I thought, There you go! 

So the next step in my thinking was, the title of the poem doesn’t have to describe what the poem is. I can write a poem called “Sonnet” that is not a sonnet at all, but it’s about the idea of a sonnet, or about poetry in general. It could start out talking about sonnets and then that would lead into Chinese poetry and it would lead into Pound and Yeats and go all over the place. 

INTERVIEWER

What do you like about sestinas? You’ve written quite a few.

WAHLE

I think the sestina form is particularly fun to play with. One thing about a sestina—this is giving away trade secrets—but if you get a good idea for one, you just need the first stanza and then the rest of the poem writes itself. At that point, you’re just filling out the form. It’s a very pretty form, or it’s intended to be. So if you write a sestina about something that’s not pretty, that’s boring, or outrageous, or silly, then the tension between the form and your content is—well, in some ways it’s the whole poem.

INTERVIEWER

You have a poem, “The Caller,” that’s a sestina about phone sex.

WAHLE

I had the idea, could you write a pornographic sestina where each of the six end-words would be an obscenity? I fiddled around with that for a while, but it was just not going anywhere. Because it was obscene for no reason. It wasn’t funny and it wasn’t interesting. And it wasn’t poetic. It wasn’t anything. So then I wrote “The Caller.” And with that, I thought, Do it another way. Think of a pornographic or semipornographic subject and then write a sestina on that subject. So then there are provocative words all the way through. You know, naked and masturbate.

That was just a complete exercise in being as outrageous as possible. You know, the poem starts out saying, “I will admit, I like to masturbate when I talk to women on the telephone.” That’s not really true. I’m not an obscene caller or anything. Part of the reason I made the title “The Caller” was to convey that this was a fictional character, even though the poem is told in the first person. But the other side of the coin is, I’ve had really intimate phone calls with women about various things. And I’ve talked to somebody on the phone when I didn’t have any clothes on or something like that. So there’s a grain of truth that I’ve exaggerated. I just exploded it into something slightly insane.

INTERVIEWER

When was the first time you disrobed during a poetry performance? 

WAHLE

I have two poems with the same title, “Naked At Last.” They’re poems about being naked, although they’re not particularly erotic. They’re more imaginative. I always thought that the way to perform those was to be naked. But I was still being fussy about such things—and I also thought I should be sitting in a chair, knees together. 

I wanted it to be obvious that I was completely nude, but not showing what Monty Python would call “the naughty bits.” I thought that would distract from the poem. I was really overthinking everything. I had all kinds of concerns about how to get on- and offstage. But then, after I’d done it, I was much more relaxed about it. As I look back at my life, I think I’ve always had an impulse toward exhibitionism. But I resisted that impulse for a long time because I didn’t want to get in trouble or offend anybody.

Photograph by Joseph Grantham.

INTERVIEWER

There’s a lot of disturbing imagery in your poems. In “The Killer on the Radio,” we have a child serial killer calmly describing his “theory of torture” on afternoon talk radio.

WAHLE

Some of my poems are spoken by people whom I would probably not admire if I knew them in real life. I don’t think I’m a very interesting person. I hope I’m an interesting writer. Maybe that’s why so many of my poems deal with such extreme subjects, including the attitudes toward sexuality, because I’ve never been impressed with myself. But I think it’s part of an artist’s responsibility to shock or rattle people. Sometimes somebody sees a play or watches a movie or reads a poem or a story, and they think, Oh my God, I would never do that. The artist should give them the chance to see that those things do exist in the world. 

INTERVIEWER

The speaker in “Secrets” is a kind of absurd confidant, assuring the reader, “You don’t have to worry. / Your secrets are safe with me.” Did you keep your poems and your performances secret from your wife? 

WAHLE

I didn’t share my work with her, but I wasn’t trying to hide anything. I was just trying to not show certain things. “Secrets” is total wacky fantasy, but it’s grounded in the fact that everybody has things they don’t want to share—they have things they don’t want certain people to know, and they have things they don’t want anybody to know. I’m not even always conscious of things that I’m keeping to myself. Sometimes it’s not even a particular decision that I’m making. In a way, maybe, I wrote that poem to keep from writing a poem about a real secret.

INTERVIEWER

Let’s talk about “A Man.” It’s a nine-line poem about a man who decides to wear a baby on his head instead of a hat. You’ve told me you don’t care for that poem.

WAHLE

Obviously, when I submitted to The Paris Review, I had some faith in it. I was probably sort of amazed when Michael Benedikt took it, but delighted. Most of the magazines I was submitting to were just tiny little offset magazines with circulations of five hundred. I was not submitting to what would’ve been considered the prestige magazines—I figured I’d be wasting the postage. I might’ve been wrong. The Paris Review was the only really good journal that I submitted to. I’m not even really sure why, other than that I liked the magazine.

Anyway, I sent that poem, they took it, I was happy. But I think it’s just very slight. For one thing, it’s a one-joke poem. I think part of what made it funny was the scatological language, which was sort of shocking but also a joke. I’m not sure I would put that in a poem now. I’ve since thought maybe it would’ve been funnier to say “pee-pee” and “poo-poo” or something. At the end of the day, the more I thought about the poem and the more it was part of my publication history, I just thought, That was really nothing. 

But if even one person likes it … and obviously more than one person liked it. You liked it. Michael Benedikt liked it. You cast your seeds into the field and see what they produce.

 

 

Joseph Grantham is the author of the poetry collections Raking Leaves and Tom Sawyer. His writing has appeared in The Believer, Bennington Review, Southwest Review, and elsewhere. With Will Patton, he edits for the small press Bohannon, which will publish its first book—a reissue of Stephen Emerson’s 1985 novel The Wife—this winter.

item.title: On “Derek,” Captain Ahab’s Evil Half Brother
item.dc:creator: John Hay
item.description: “Your worst enemy ain’t Moby Dick, it’s your half brother, Derek.”
item.content:encoded:
Still from The Sea Beast (1926), Grosset & Dunlap photoplay edition. Public domain, courtesy of John Hay.

The Sea Beast, the first film adaptation of Moby-Dick, begins with a leather-bound edition of the novel opening to page one, but the phrase “Call me Ishmael” is nowhere to be found. That’s because there’s no Ishmael in this movie at all. Instead, theatergoers a hundred years ago were introduced to a new character: Captain Ahab’s evil younger brother, Derek. Yes, Derek.

This silent film, released in 1926, offers the story of a dreamy and handsome young harpooner named Ahab Ceeley, cut down in his prime by both fraternal and cetaceous violence. The Hollywood leading man John Barrymore plays Ahab as a valiant lover, wooing the beautiful Esther with his nautical prowess and igniting the envy of his jealous half brother, who hopes to steal Esther’s heart. The dastardly Derek stealthily shoves his sibling into the jaws of a vicious sperm whale, then convinces the now-disabled Ahab that his sweetheart could never accept him in his disfigured condition. Plunged into a steely despair, the captain focuses his hate on the legendary Moby Dick—at least until he discovers the truth. “Your worst enemy ain’t Moby Dick,” a sailor eventually informs him, “it’s your half brother, Derek.”

Warner Bros. poster for The Sea Beast, via Wikimedia Commons (left). Bess Meredyth, Motion Picture News, via Internet Archive (right). Public domain.

Derek is not an obscure detail in Herman Melville’s 1851 masterpiece. He does not appear in the book at all. He was, rather, a wild departure from Melville’s text, an invention credited to veteran “scenarist” Bess Meredyth, at the behest of Hollywood producers, in a bid to add flashy, dramatic conflict to the metaphysical profundities of the novel. Movie adaptations of maritime adventures were hot in the twenties; then-familiar films such as The Sea Wolf (1920) and The Sea Hawk (1924), based on books by Jack London and Rafael Sabatini, had also featured evil brothers, and the Warners’ title change to The Sea Beast capitalized on this association. Similarly, the introduction of a romantic triangle, while a strange addition to the source text, wasn’t atypical for that era; Meredyth’s son later noted that his mother knew the love story was odd but “surrendered to the studio’s request” to introduce it. And perhaps unsurprising for Old Hollywood—though ridiculous to anyone who’s read the novel—The Sea Beast has a happy ending: Ahab manages to kill both Derek and the white whale in quick succession, and then returns to find Esther waiting for him with tears of joy.

Warner Bros. promotional booklet for The Sea Beast. Photograph by John Hay.

This was neither the first nor the last time that a movie studio would grossly distort a literary classic. But Derek is an especially unusual figure in the history of Moby-Dick, not merely because he represented such a stark departure from the book but because he played an integral role in popularizing the text in the twenties and thirties, thus cementing its enduring appeal. As late as 1980, the director John Huston complained that Gregory Peck’s portrayal of Ahab in his own 1956 film adaptation of Moby-Dick was unfairly criticized by viewers because “the John Barrymore version of Ahab” had “colored it forever for audiences.” And this immortal Barrymore version was the one with Derek.

George O’Hara as Derek in two stills from The Sea Beast (1926). Public domain, courtesy of John Hay.

Only a decade earlier, Moby-Dick had been relatively unknown. Melville’s reputation had dwindled to obscurity in his later years; when he died in 1891, the New York Times ran a brief notice that called him “an absolutely forgotten man.” But in 1919, when a Columbia professor serving as an editor at The Nation, Carl Van Doren, commissioned a junior colleague to write a reconsideration of Melville for his centenary, the piece extolled the extraordinary genius of an unappreciated author. Van Doren himself admired Moby-Dick, but he suspected that the dense whaling novel would never find a large audience, writing in 1921 that it was “too irregular, too bizarre, perhaps, ever to win the most popular suffrage.”

Van Doren was wrong on this point. The Nation piece led not just to a reconsideration but to a veritable rebirth. Over the next decade, critics across the country began to sing the praises of an overlooked virtuoso, and Melville’s books (whose copyrights had expired) quickly found their way back into print. Scholars now refer to this phenomenon of the twenties as the “Melville Revival,” a moment when the obscure writer suddenly became canonical and Moby-Dick became a candidate for the Great American Novel.

Warner Bros. promotional booklet for The Sea Beast. Photograph by John Hay.

Yet for all the encomiums by English professors, nothing promoted Melville’s profile more than The Sea Beast. When the film debuted in January of 1926, theaters were sold out for weeks both in the United States and abroad. During the film’s New York City run, Wanamaker’s department store hosted a Moby-Dick week with displays of whaling relics, lectures on whaling history, and performances of sea chanteys. Notably, patrons could also purchase the novel. In the silent-film era, popular movies could offer giant boosts to book sales; savvy publishers understood that viewers often wanted to read the narration and dialogue only implied on the screen. The firm Grosset & Dunlap quickly cornered the market on “photoplay” editions by reprinting literary texts alongside stills from their film adaptations and packaging them in attractive new dust jackets.

The cover of Grosset & Dunlap’s 1926 edition of Moby-Dick explicitly advertised its connection to The Sea Beast, even featuring a “signed” picture of John Barrymore as Ahab. The text itself is Melville’s novel—no Derek, no love interest, no happy ending. But the accompanying photographs suggest that readers should also be aware of the movie’s plot. One passage explaining how the cabin boy, Pip, loses his mind in the heartless immensity of the ocean is awkwardly juxtaposed next to a photo of Ahab and Derek in a tavern. The caption reads: “His Brother—‘a Treacherous, Kindless Villain’ Deceives the Unfortunate, Trusting Ahab.” 

Some readers must have been confused by this picture of an unknown character, captioned with a phrase taken, inexplicably, from Hamlet. But any concerns would surely have been assuaged by the short publisher’s preface, which argued that the Warner Bros. adaptation actually “exceeds the book” in brilliance. Melville’s shortcoming, the preface claimed, was in attributing Ahab’s insanity to a single, isolated injury—an unconvincing determinant since, of course, people lose limbs all the time without becoming maniacs. Thus, the publisher concluded, the film’s addition of a lost sweetheart and a perfidious brother was “not presumptuous meddling” but rather “a laudable act of critical explanation”—a means of making Ahab’s madness more believable. Problem solved!

Grosset & Dunlap photoplay edition (left); Readers Library novelization (center); Big Little Book easy reader (right). Photographs by John Hay.

The literary tie-ins did not stop there. Following the film’s successful overseas run, a London publishing firm called the Readers Library put out its own novelization of The Sea Beast. This one was not the 1851 novel but a faithful adaptation of the 1926 film, transforming the screenplay back into book form. While the authors, Hayter Preston and Henry Savage, occasionally adopted snippets of Melville’s prose (“I’d strike the sun if it insulted me”), they took special care to describe the evil machinations and “darkening brow” of Derek: “In Ahab’s utter vanquishment he was drinking joy to the very lees.” (The Readers Library later claimed, improbably, that this novelization sold some two hundred thousand copies.)

Lloyd Hughes as Derek in Moby Dick (193o). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Derek, kept alive by these new publications, didn’t disappear. In 1930, Warner Bros. put out a “talkie” remake of The Sea Beast, retitled Moby Dick, which proved another hit. They reshot the film with different actors, save for John Barrymore, who remained in his starring role. The cruel Derek, played by the hammy Lloyd Hughes, could now vocally express his malice: “I hate you,” he screams at Ahab in a climactic fraternal fistfight, “worse than you hate that whale!” 

Grosset & Dunlap promptly republished their photoplay version of Melville’s novel, substituting new stills from the 1930 film, just as ill-fitting as they’d been before. Even as late as 1934, the Wisconsin-based Big Little Book children’s series—known for its editions of Dick Tracy and Little Orphan Annie—released The Story of Moby Dick, an easy-to-read novelization mash-up of both the 1926 silent film and the 1930 talkie, with a still from The Sea Beast on every other page. Oddly, Ahab’s evil brother appears here as “Dereck”—perhaps to emphasize that he is pure dreck.

Even if you believe that creating a sinister sibling adds needed drama to Moby-Dick, the choice of name still rings false. Ahab, after all, is supposedly from a Nantucket Quaker community fond of Old Testament nomenclature; “Derek” is clearly a misfit, most likely introduced to play on anti-German sentiments following the First World War. 

Meredyth, though, could claim a hint of textual justification. In chapter 81 of Melville’s novel (“The Pequod Meets the Virgin”), Ahab’s mates effectively outhunt the crew of the German whaler Jungfrau, captained by a comically inept skipper named Derick De Deer. In an easy-to-miss moment, the foolish Germans row away after an uncatchably swift finback whale, mistaking it for a slower sperm whale. The chapter concludes with a gentle admonition: “Oh! many are the Fin-Backs, and many are the Dericks, my friend.”

 

John Hay is a professor in the Department of English at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. His writing has appeared in Public Books and the Los Angeles Review of Books, among other publications. He is the editor of the Las Vegas Review of Books.

item.title: Adelle Waldman Is the 2026–2027 Paris Review Visiting Professor at the Bard Prison Initiative
item.dc:creator: The Paris Review
item.description: “In 2024, The Paris Review and BPI announced a partnership, through which a distinguished creative writer would teach the literature that has most inspired them to BPI’s students.”
item.content:encoded:
Photograph by Lou Rouse.

We are delighted to announce that Adelle Waldman is the 2026–2027 Paris Review Visiting Professor at the Bard Prison Initiative (BPI).

BPI has provided a full-time, tuition-free liberal arts education to students incarcerated at several upstate New York prisons since 1999, and currently enrolls more than four hundred students across seven campuses; it also offers tuition-free degree programs through the Bard Microcolleges, hosted at local institutions such as the Brooklyn Public Library. In 2024, The Paris Review and BPI announced a partnership, through which a distinguished creative writer would teach the literature that has most inspired them to BPI’s students. Waldman succeeds Javier Fuentes, and will teach three semester-long courses over the next year.

Waldman’s 2013 novel, The Love Affairs of Nathaniel P., which updates the comedy of manners for the modern age, was widely celebrated for its wry commentary on the mores of contemporary Brooklyn. In 2018, Waldman moved to upstate New York and began working part-time at Target, where she unloaded trucks at 4 A.M.; the experience inspired her second novel, Help Wanted, a polyphonic work told through the perspectives of several employees at a big-box store.

Waldman’s first course focuses on Jane Austen—an author whose unsparing wit and keen social observations are a model for Waldman’s own, and whose characters cannot help but provide endless fodder for speculation, even gossip. “Society has changed so much, yet we still feel as if we know these people,” Waldman says. “The Austen scholar and the first-time reader are both equally qualified to form a considered opinion as to, say, how much we should forgive Emma for her mistakes, or which of the Dashwood sisters Austen favors in Sense and Sensibility.” Classes began in September.
